evidence: Kew/POWO accepts Ulmus americana and lists Texas in its native range.
Hays County — the project Hays County native-source list includes U. americana.
Bell County — USDA ARS Biocollections preserves multiple 2014 specimens collected at the Little River near Little River-Academy.
Travis County — USDA ARS Biocollections preserves a 2014 U. americana specimen from Redbud Island, Austin.
target_zone_range.guardrail: Bell and Travis are herbarium collection records interpreted within a source-confirmed native Texas range; planted street-tree records are not used.

morphology.look_here_first: Start with the big asymmetric leaf and the spring samara: American elm has relatively large double-serrate leaves with a strongly uneven base, then a flat oval samara with a ciliate margin and a deep apical notch.
diagnostic_traits: large deciduous elm, often developing a vase-shaped crown
leaves mostly >7 cm, ovate to elliptic with strongly oblique base
lower leaf surface glabrous to pubescent, often with tufts in vein axils
flowers before leaf-out in spring on slender pedicels
oval spring samara with seed near center, ciliate margin, and a deep apical notch

confusers.separator: Slippery elm has red-tomentose bud-scale margins, much rougher thick leaves, and a samara pubescent on the body rather than a ciliate margin.
Winged elm has smaller leaves and conspicuous regular corky wings on branches; American elm lacks those wings.
Cedar elm has much smaller rough leaves and reproduces in fall rather than spring.
